news.title: Secretary of Education Linda McMahon Issues a Nationwide Call to Commemorate the 25th Anniversary of the 9/11 Terrorist Attacks with America’s Students
news.content:
September 10, 2026
Today, U.S. Secretary of Education Linda McMahon issued a nationwide call to action, urging K-12 educators across the country to set aside time tomorrow to honor the victims and heroes of the September 11th terrorist attacks on its 25th anniversary.
In her message to teachers and education leaders, the Secretary highlighted the importance of ensuring younger generations understand the history, the profound loss, and the extraordinary courage that shaped the nation’s response. As today’s students were born long after the attacks, Secretary McMahon encouraged schools to help bridge this gap through thoughtful, age‑appropriate civic instruction.
“A quarter century has passed since that terrible day, but we must never forget what September 11th means for the United States,”
wrote U.S. Secretary of Education Linda McMahon.
“This year, I call on American schools to educate students with moral clarity about the events of that day and its significance for the Nation’s history. Educators can achieve this by incorporating an age-appropriate lesson about 9/11, a moment of silence to mark the time the first plane struck the World Trade Center, or by asking students to share their own reflections about that tragic day.”
Secretary McMahon prompted educators to ground lessons in the real stories of individuals whose courage continues to define the legacy of 9/11 — such as the passengers of United Flight 93, Welles Crowther (the “Man in the Red Bandana”), and Lieutenant Colonel Marilyn Wills.
To bring classrooms across the country together in remembrance, the Secretary invited every school to participate in a moment of silence tomorrow. This observance honors the 2,977 victims, the heroic first responders, the service members who gave their lives in the years that followed, and the families who continue to carry their legacy forward.
“I encourage every school in the nation to join me in observing a
moment of silence
tomorrow and play your part in fulfilling the promise to
Never Forget
,”
concluded Secretary McMahon.

news.title: Building Strong Readers: How the Trump Administration is Supercharging Evidence-Based Literacy to Combat Reading Crisis
news.content:
September 9, 2026
America is facing a literacy emergency that is reshaping the trajectory of an entire generation. National reading scores – long a bellwether for student success – have dropped to historic lows.
Twelfth graders today have the lowest reading scores ever recorded, and nearly 70% of 4th and 8th graders cannot read proficiently.
A recent international
assessment
revealed America’s lowest-performing students are falling further behind – and have suffered a loss of learning in reading equivalent to nearly a year and a half of instruction compared to 2015.
In response, the Trump Department of Education (the Department) has made literacy a central priority across its grantmaking, research agenda, and technical assistance efforts.
Federal dollars are no longer flowing on autopilot.
Nor is taxpayer money being expended to drive the divisive DEI efforts of the prior Administration that detract from fundamental priorities like literacy. Instead, the Department is focusing its investments on proven approaches grounded in the Science of Reading. By strengthening state capacity in teacher preparation for evidence-based literacy and prioritizing materials aligned with phonics instruction, the Trump Administration is empowering states to overhaul their literacy ecosystems.
Investing in Proven Solutions
Across multiple grant programs, the Department is leveraging the Secretary’s
literacy priority
to fund approaches that have a demonstrated impact on student reading nationwide. Although these funds would be best spent directly by states, the Trump Administration is ensuring that all taxpayer dollars are spent responsibly and directed toward meaningful learning. To the end, existing grant funding will support the Secretary’s literacy priority through:
Education Innovation and Research (EIR) Grants:
These
grants
support furthered research on and in support of tutoring models, effective instructional programs, and professional development aligned with the Science of Reading. Over the past two years, the Department has awarded
nearly $500 million through 49 grants.
Of these grants,
a record 17 were awarded to state educational agencies,
enabling them to take the lead in researching, implementing, and scaling effective literacy practices statewide.
Teacher Quality Partnership (TQP) Grants:
These
grants
are intended to help colleges and school districts prepare teachers to deliver strong literacy instruction. In the coming weeks, the Department anticipates
awarding 12 new TQP grants, totaling roughly $70 million.
Supporting Effective Educator Development (SEED Grants) Grants:
These
grants
support educator certification pathways and literacy coaching. In the coming weeks, the Department anticipates
awarding 16 new SEED grants, totaling roughly $90 million.
Innovative Approaches to Literacy (IAL) Grants:
These
grants
help improve early literacy from birth through grade 5 – including expanding book access, boosting at-home literacy, and building teacher skills. This week, leveraging the Secretary’s priority in evidence-based literacy,
the Department awarded four new IAL grants, totaling more than $16 million.
Comprehensive Literacy State Development (CLSD) Grants:
These
grants
support states and other jurisdictions to develop statewide literacy plans, improve teacher prep, buy high‑quality materials, and deploy literacy coaches. This year, the Department provided $256 million in non-competing continuation awards to 24 states, the Outlying Areas, and the Bureau of Indian Education.
National Center on Academic Interventions:
The Department is awarding $3.7 million for this
grant
program which provides support for improving outcomes for students with disabilities, with evidence‑based literacy instruction as a required component.
Strengthening Research & Tools for Educators
The Department’s research arm (IES) is
refocusing
its largest Fiscal Year 2027 grants to fund actionable projects in areas of national need identified by the states, with
literacy as a core priority
. At the same time, IES Regional Educational Labs have developed
practical toolkits for teachers
– covering K–3 reading comprehension, differentiating early reading instruction, and interventions for grades 6–8. These tools give educators ready to use strategies that are backed by evidence.
The Bottom Line
The Trump Administration is directing federal dollars toward strategies proven to help children read – and giving states the tools, flexibility, and support to rebuild strong literacy outcomes. Rather than spending hard-earned taxpayer dollars on ineffective initiatives or DEI-laden programs, the Trump Administration is making sure every dollar spent supports effective, evidence-based literacy instruction.

news.title: What They Are Saying: Pilot States Highlight Early Successes with the Learning Agenda Playbook
news.content:
September 9, 2026
Following the
Learning Agenda Playbook (the Playbook)
release this morning, state leaders from the eight pilot states praised the framework as a resource to improve state education policies, programs, and student outcomes.
The Playbook
marks a pivotal milestone in returning education to the states and driving improvements at the state and local levels.
Click
here
for more information about
the Playbook.
Click
here
to view
the Playbook.
Arkansas Secretary of Education Jacob Oliva:
“Arkansas is proud to partner with the Department, alongside other states, to identify problems of practice and develop lasting solutions. This Playbook will help drive improved outcomes for all students by advancing a unified accountability approach and strengthening coordinated support across our education system.”
Georgia State School Superintendent Richard Woods:
"Too often, states are asked to do 'just one more thing,' adding paperwork and administrative burdens that do little to improve outcomes for students. What makes this work different is that it helps us focus on the 'one thing' that matters most. In Georgia, this project is helping us build better systems and connect more meaningfully with those closest to the work — our teachers, students, families, and other stakeholders — as we implement our core goals. We appreciate the U.S. Department of Education's commitment to investing in states as they implement their strategic priorities. Ultimately, we know this work will help us ensure that every action we take as an agency has the greatest possible impact where it matters most: in the classroom."
Idaho Superintendent of Public Instruction Debbie Critchfield:
“The development of Idaho’s Learning Agenda has provided a framework for evaluating the impact of our initiatives and priorities while strengthening our data-driven decision-making. This pilot has also improved communication across our teams and better aligned our efforts around our student outcome goals. That connection helps ensure the work we do is focused, coordinated and ultimately making a difference for Idaho students.”
Kansas Commissioner of Education Dr. Jake Steel:
“We are grateful for the opportunity to participate as a pilot state in the Learning Agenda Initiative. This work gave Kansas dedicated time and support to bring people together around a coherent approach to school improvement and better align our priorities, resources, research and evaluation. Learning alongside other states strengthened our work and will help us make evidence-based decisions, continuously improve our efforts and achieve better outcomes for Kansas students.”
New Hampshire Commissioner of Education Caitlin Davis:
“The Learning Agenda process has been an important part of our work at the New Hampshire Department of Education. As a pilot state, it gave us a structured opportunity to step back, ask the right questions, and use evidence to sharpen our priorities and direction. This has been especially helpful as we develop New Hampshire’s new statewide literacy plan and identify the strategies that will have the greatest impact on student achievement. Through this work, we have also connected with partners in other states that have undertaken similar efforts and learned a great deal from their experiences. The Learning Agenda has helped us better align our work and establish a strong foundation for improving outcomes across the state. We appreciate the U.S. Department of Education for giving New Hampshire the opportunity to participate.
Tennessee Commissioner of Education Lizzette Reynolds:
“Tennessee’s participation in the Learning Agenda initiative is an exciting opportunity to ensure we have the right information aligned with TDOE priorities and to identify practical solutions to current challenges. By highlighting powerful stories of impact and effective practices across our state, we can motivate educators and stakeholders to replicate what works best for students nationwide. This commitment to continuous improvement will help drive sustained progress in education.”
Utah Superintendent of Public Instruction Dr. Molly Hart:
"Developing data-driven solutions is essential to meeting the unique needs of our students and schools. Partnering in the development of the Learning Agenda Playbook has helped strengthen our state's capacity to turn research into actionable, impact-focused strategies. We are proud to support this tool to help education leaders nationwide use evidence to strengthen student success."
Wisconsin Superintendent of Public Instruction Dr. Jill Underly:
“The learning agenda presented Wisconsin with an opportunity to add capacity to our state's existing strategic plan, specifically around early childhood. We were able to map data and systems to plan for change that better aligns the multiple agencies and partners working to serve young children. It also reinforced alignment with all of Wisconsin's technical assistance partners.”

news.title: U.S. Department of Education Launches Learning Agenda Playbook to Support State Education Leaders and Improve Student Outcomes
news.content:
September 9, 2026
As the Trump Administration works to return education to the states, the U.S. Department of Education (the Department) today unveiled the
Learning Agenda Playbook (the Playbook)
, a resource developed alongside states to strengthen their capacity, enable them to take greater ownership of education, and drive improvement at the state and local levels.
Returning education to the states means ensuring state leaders have the tools to identify their own priorities, use evidence to determine what works best for their students and communities, and then direct resources accordingly. By strengthening states’ ability to make evidence-based decisions independently,
the Playbook
helps shift education away from Washington, D.C. and closer to the students, families, educators, and communities they serve.
The Playbook
brings fundamental tools together in one place for states:
Facilitator’s Guide:
a step-by-step resource for those supporting state teams through the
Learning Agenda
process;
Facilitator’s Toolbox:
slides, exercises, and worksheets that support hands-on implementation;
Learning Agenda Template:
a structured format to guide states in the development of their own agendas; and
Capacity Continuum:
a tool to help states assess current capabilities and identify areas for growth.
“As the monumental shift to return education to the states continues, the Trump Administration is ensuring state leaders have the tools and support necessary to take on this expanded role with confidence,”
said U.S. Secretary of Education Linda McMahon.
“The
Learning Agenda Playbook
delivers a rigorous, field-tested framework of best practices, eliminating the need for states to reinvent the wheel. With a clear process and proven tools, states can lead more boldly and drive better outcomes for students and families.”
Background:
A
Learning Agenda
is a strategic, multi-year plan that guides SEAs to identify their most pressing challenges, ask the right questions, build the evidence to answer them, and invest state resources where they will have the greatest impact.
The U.S. Department of Education, through the Office of Elementary and Secondary Education and the Institute of Education Sciences and in collaboration with the National Comprehensive Center, worked alongside eight state educational agencies to develop, test, and refine the
Learning Agenda Playbook.
Participating states included: Arkansas, Georgia, Idaho, Kansas, New Hampshire, Tennessee, Utah, and Wisconsin.
The goal is not more data, but better evidence to drive better decisions and, most importantly, stronger outcomes for students.
